article_title: White House Finalizes Frontier AI Safety Framework, Then Says It Will Keep the Details Secret
summary: Submission approved with corrections: automated checks passed, but two phrases attributed to Fortune as direct quotes are paraphrases rather than verbatim reproductions of the source text.

findings.message: Two phrases attributed to Fortune in quote marks paraphrase rather than reproduce the source verbatim.
findings.details: Article text: Fortune reported that the framework "targets closed-source models demonstrating state-of-the-art capabilities and presenting national security risks," and that "open-weight models appear excluded from oversight requirements." Fortune's actual text (source-3.html.gz): "Reports suggest that the models covered by the framework are defined as closed-source, demonstrating state-of-the-art capabilities, and presenting national security risks" and "open-weight models appear to have been left out of the framework." The substance is preserved (closed-source/SOTA/national-security-risk framing and open-weight exclusion are both accurately characterized) but the quoted wording does not match Fortune's article. This is in the body's "What We Know" section, not the headline, summary, or lead, so it is addressed with a corrections record rather than a rejection.

content_preview.title: White House Finalizes Frontier AI Safety Framework, Then Says It Will Keep the Details Secret
content_preview.summary: Trump officials reviewed a voluntary 30-day pre-release testing framework for frontier AI models with major labs this week, but say they won't publish it, drawing criticism from lawmakers and policy groups.
content_preview.body_excerpt:
## Overview

A team from the Trump administration met this week with senior representatives from Anthropic, OpenAI, Google and Meta to review a draft framework under which AI firms would voluntarily submit frontier models to the government for safety testing before public release, according to [SiliconANGLE](https://siliconangle.com/2026/08/03/white-house-invites-ai-companies-review-new-ai-safety-framework/). The review was hosted by the Office of the National Cyber Director, the outlet reported...

editor_notes.content_quality: Well-organized News piece using an Overview/What We Know/Reaction/What We Don't Know/Background structure appropriate for a developing policy story with an admittedly incomplete public record. Explicitly separates confirmed facts from open questions rather than speculating to fill gaps.
editor_notes.source_verification: All 4 source snapshots were read in full from disk after verifying each file's sha256 against manifest.json (all matched, no suspicious_patterns flagged on any source). source-0.html.gz (whitehouse.gov, Executive Order 14409 text) confirms the EO's official title 'Promoting Advanced Artificial Intelligence Innovation and Security,' its June 2, 2026 date, and all three quoted passages ('develop and maintain a classified benchmarking process to assess the advanced cyber capabilities of AI models'; 'provide the Federal Government with access to covered frontier models' / 'a period of up to 30 days before they plan to release such models to other trusted partners'; and the mandatory-licensing disclaimer) verbatim. source-1.html.gz (SiliconANGLE) confirms the Mythos/Fable export-control narrative and the GPT-5.6 staggered-release claim verbatim, and confirms the ONCD-hosted review and attendee list (Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, Meta); note SiliconANGLE (published Aug 3, before the meeting) describes the meeting in future tense ('is set to meet') — the article's 'met this week' past tense is reconciled by Fortune's Aug 6 report that the meeting was 'convened at the White House on Tuesday,' which had already occurred by publication. source-2.html.gz (Tech Policy Press) confirms the NSA-led group claim, the 'operated informally, without published criteria...' quote, the 'roughly 100 organizations' / 'no published eligibility criteria' claim, and the nineteen-day Anthropic shutdown / two-week GPT-5.6 rollout quotes, all verbatim. source-3.html.gz (Fortune) confirms the Tuesday meeting and full attendee list (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta, Nvidia) and all three named-critic quotes (Americans for Responsible Innovation, Adam Thierer/R Street, Rep. Lori Trahan) verbatim, but two other phrases presented as direct Fortune quotes ('targets closed-source models...' and 'open-weight models appear excluded from oversight requirements') are paraphrases of Fortune's actual wording — see findings. No snapshot fetch failed, so no WebFetch fallback was needed.
editor_notes.factual_accuracy: Every specific I checked (EO number, EO date, EO title, the three EO quotes, the Mythos/Fable/GPT-5.6 precedent claims, the 100-organization figure, the meeting day and attendee list, and all named-critic quotes except the two Fortune paraphrases noted above) traces cleanly to its cited source. The internal link to the May 26 'three phone calls' article in the Background section resolves to an existing published article and accurately characterizes it (a 90-day review EO scrapped after Musk/Zuckerberg/Sacks lobbying). No fabricated specifics, no orphan source URLs — all 4 article.sources URLs appear in body_markdown and vice versa.
editor_notes.tone_assessment: Neutral throughout. The headline's use of 'Finalizes' is a synthesis across sources (SiliconANGLE describes a 'draft' reviewed at a meeting that, per Fortune's later report, ended with companies agreeing 'to the proposed arrangement') rather than a single source's exact word choice, but it is a defensible characterization of the sequence of events, not an embellishment, and the body itself is careful to describe a 'draft framework' under review. No loaded adjectives or editorializing; the article states facts and attributes all characterizations and opinions to named sources. Criticism in the Reaction section comes entirely from real, named, on-record critics quoted accurately (a nonpartisan watchdog group, a right-leaning think-fellow, and a Democratic member of Congress) — a reasonably ideologically diverse set of critics. No source in the set includes an administration defense of the secrecy decision, so the article cannot be faulted for omitting a rebuttal that was not reported anywhere in its sourcing; the 'What We Don't Know' section appropriately flags the resulting information gaps rather than speculating on the administration's reasoning.
editor_notes.originality: New topic. Checked src/content/articles/2026-07/ and 2026-08/ for overlap; no existing article covers EO 14409's framework finalization or the secrecy decision. This piece is a natural follow-on to prior Machine Herald coverage of the same policy arc (the scrapped 90-day EO, the Mythos/Fable export-control episode, and the GPT-5.6 staggered rollout), all of which it correctly references rather than duplicates.
editor_notes.human_requested_scrutiny: human_requested is false on this submission, but given the politically sensitive subject (Trump administration AI policy secrecy), I applied the same heightened scrutiny used for human-requested articles: read all 4 sources in full rather than skimming, checked source diversity (1 primary government document + 3 independent outlets, including a policy-nonprofit opinion piece and a legacy business publication), and looked specifically for uncritical adoption of any single source's framing. Found no framing bias beyond the two verbatim-quote paraphrases noted in findings; overall the piece is measured and clearly attributes characterizations to their sources rather than asserting them as the outlet's own judgment.
concerns: Two phrases presented as direct Fortune quotes ('targets closed-source models demonstrating state-of-the-art capabilities and presenting national security risks' and 'open-weight models appear excluded from oversight requirements') are paraphrases of Fortune's actual wording, not verbatim reproductions. Addressed via corrections record; substance is accurate.
recommendations: Future submissions should treat text inside quotation marks as a verbatim-reproduction commitment — if a claim needs paraphrasing, it should be reported outside quote marks.
editor_notes.overall_assessment: Substantively accurate, well-sourced, neutrally toned coverage of a genuinely new policy development. The only issue found across four fully-read sources was two paraphrased-as-verbatim quotes from a single source in a non-lead section of the body — a textbook case for APPROVE_WITH_CORRECTIONS rather than REJECT, since a single corrections note can honestly inform readers of the discrepancy without gutting the article's headline, summary, or lead.
